newsitem.title: USA: Tight arb lifts sweet foreign crudes in U.S. Gulf.
newsitem.headline: Tight arb lifts sweet foreign crudes in U.S. Gulf.

text.p: The tight trans-Atlantic arbitrage lifted sweet foreign crude prices on Thursday, causing buyers to pause after a flurry of purchases earlier in the week, traders said.
North Sea Brent crude was notionally assessed at October West Texas Intermediate/Cushing even to minus five cents a barrel for one million barrels delivered into the Gulf, traders said.
Brent offered off a VLCC carrying around two million barrels would be cheaper at WTI minus 15-20 cents a barrel.
The clincher for sellers, however, was the rising cost of freight.
"Freight rates have really climbed," a North Sea player said. "When the Iraqi barrels came out, all the ships got picked up."

No companies were actively showing Brent into the Gulf, even as the price for dated cargoes swung wildly in Europe from September Brent minus five cents to September Brent minus 29 cents for August loaders.
"The real price is probably somewhere in between," an East Coast trader said.
On the screens, the September spread between WTI and Brent was around 85-90 cents a barrel on Thursday afternoon, down sharply from around $1.20-1.30 in recent weeks.
In Latin America, sellers were beginning to toughen up on their offers for Colombian Cusiana after several deals were done between $1.05 and $1.10 under October WTI earlier this week, traders said.
Sellers were now asking 90 cents to $1.00 under the benchmark for the coveted grade.
"The sellers figured out that Brent isn't coming over here," a Gulf trader said.
From West Africa, traders said Asian demand remained strong, although several cargoes were still looking for homes in the Gulf.
A U.S. company was offering Nigerian Qua Iboe for September 18-22 arrival, asking Dated Brent plus $1.87 a barrel.
The remaining late August arrivals, including a late August Brass River, were finally cleaned up, traders said.
The general foreign crude market in the Gulf was seen as tightening. "There's a lot of barrels out there, but everyone wants them in the same timeframe," a trader said.
